newsitem.title: CUBA: Cuba says economy will grow despite sugar harvest.
newsitem.headline: Cuba says economy will grow despite sugar harvest.

text.p: Cuban vice-president Carlos Lage said on Sunday the economy was set to grow this year despite lower than expected sugar cane production in the last harvest.
The Cuban news agency Prensa Latina quoted Lage as saying the economy was still recovering but did not provide a forecast for this year's Gross Domestic Product (GDP) growth.
Officials on the communist-ruled island have said recently they expect GDP growth to reach its targeted four to five percent in 1997, compared with 7.8 percent growth last year.
But outside observers and some independent economists are sceptical this target can be met, partly because of the poorer than expected sugar harvest.

Lage, speaking in the eastern city of Santiago de Cuba, gave no figures but said there had been growth in the first six months of the year in tourism, nickel mining, fisheries and tobacco production, all of which are key foreign exchange earners, while sugar production was down.

No official figure has been given for the 1996-97 sugar harvest that ended earlier this month. But experts expect production will be about 4.2 million tonnes, below the government's original forecast of a modest improvement on 1995-96 production of 4.45 million tonnes.

Lage said various factors contributed to the sugar shortfall, including inefficiency and poor organisation, as well as a hurricane that swept the island last October and delays to foreign financing for technical input to the sector.

Cuba's economy has posted modest growth since 1995 after a severe recession caused by the collapse of the former Soviet Union, but the standard of living in Cuba is still well below what it was in the 1980s.
